title: “DON’T JUDGE ME!” — BUT JESUS SAID SOMETHING ELSE THAT MOST PEOPLE NEVER QUOTE
paragraphs: “DON’T JUDGE ME!” — BUT JESUS SAID SOMETHING ELSE THAT MOST PEOPLE NEVER QUOTE
The Forgotten Command in John 7:24 That Exposes Religious Hypocrisy, Confronts Hidden Sin, and Reveals Why Real Love Refuses to Call Darkness Light
There is a sentence that can silence an entire room of Christians.
Three words.
“Don’t judge me.”

Say those words at the right moment, and suddenly everyone becomes uncomfortable. The conversation changes. The person who spoke the truth starts questioning whether they should have said anything at all.
And somewhere in the silence, a Bible verse appears.
“Judge not, that ye be not judged.” — Matthew 7:1 (KJV)
Conversation over.
Or so we think.
Because there is another statement from Jesus that rarely gets mentioned in that moment.
A statement so direct, so uncomfortable, and so misunderstood that it forces both the person confronting sin and the person defending it to examine their hearts.
“Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.” — John 7:24 (KJV)
Read that again.
Jesus did not merely warn against judging.
He also commanded righteous judgment.
And before you use that verse to confront somebody else's sin, there is something you need to understand.
The same Jesus who told us to judge righteously also told us to remove the beam from our own eye.
That means this passage is not a weapon for self-righteous Christians.
And it is not permission for unrepentant Christians to hide behind the language of grace.
It is a confrontation with both.
Because sometimes the person shouting “Don't judge me!” is running from conviction.
And sometimes the person shouting “Repent!” is running from the truth about their own heart.
Jesus sees both.
And He loves both too much to leave either one unchanged.
Imagine a woman sitting alone in her car after Sunday worship.
Her Bible is on the passenger seat.
The sermon is still echoing in her mind.
Her phone lights up.
It is a message from someone she knows she should not be entertaining.
She stares at the screen.
She knows the relationship is pulling her away from obedience to Christ. She has prayed about it. She has cried about it. She has promised God she would walk away.
But loneliness has a way of making disobedience feel like comfort.
She reaches for the phone.
Then she remembers what her Christian friend told her earlier that week.
“You know this isn't leading you toward Jesus.”
She had responded immediately.
“Don't judge me. God knows my heart.”
And He does.
That is precisely what makes those words so serious.
God knows the heartbreak beneath her choices. He knows the wounds, the abandonment, the nights she begged Him to take away the loneliness.
But He also knows when she is using those wounds to justify something He is calling her to surrender.
He sees the pain.
He sees the compromise.
And He does not confuse compassion with approval.
Now imagine the friend who confronted her.
He goes home after telling her to repent.
He opens his Bible, feeling satisfied that he defended righteousness.

But his own marriage is deteriorating because of his harshness. He has become comfortable with gossip. He speaks about other people's failures with an enthusiasm he never shows when confessing his own.
He is right about the danger of sin.
But something is wrong with his spirit.
He knows how to identify darkness in someone else's life.
He has forgotten how to kneel before God about the darkness in his own.
Two people.
Two different spiritual dangers.
One hiding behind “Don't judge me.”
The other hiding behind “I'm just speaking the truth.”
And Jesus confronts them both.
This is where John 7:24 becomes more than a verse to win an argument.
It becomes a mirror.
To understand it, we must return to the scene where Jesus actually spoke those words.

In John chapter 7, Jesus was teaching in Jerusalem during the Feast of Tabernacles. His authority and actions were being questioned. The controversy involved, among other things, His healing of a man on the Sabbath, an event described earlier in John chapter 5.
Some religious leaders considered His Sabbath healing a violation of their understanding of the law.
Jesus exposed the inconsistency in their reasoning.
They accepted circumcision on the Sabbath in obedience to the Mosaic law, yet became angry when He made an entire man well on the Sabbath.
Then He said:
“Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.” — John 7:24 (KJV)
The original Greek reads:
μὴ κρίνετε κατ’ ὄψιν, ἀλλὰ τὴν δικαίαν κρίσιν κρίνατε.
Transliterated:
Mē krinete kat’ opsin, alla tēn dikaian krisin krinate.
A close translation is:
“Do not judge according to appearance, but judge with righteous judgment.”
The Greek verb κρίνω (krinō) can mean to judge, evaluate, distinguish, or decide, depending on context.
The expression κατ’ ὄψιν (kat’ opsin) refers to judging according to outward appearance.
And δικαίαν κρίσιν (dikaian krisin) means righteous or just judgment.
Notice what Jesus was correcting.
He was not encouraging His listeners to become spiritual detectives, constantly searching for someone to condemn.
He was confronting superficial and unjust evaluation.
They were judging His actions without rightly understanding the law, the circumstances, or the purpose of His work.
They had religious knowledge.
But their judgment was distorted.
And here is the uncomfortable question.
How often do we make the same mistake while believing we are defending God?
We see a person with tattoos and assume rebellion.
We see a struggling single mother and assume irresponsibility.
We see a believer battling addiction and assume there is no genuine faith.
We see someone who has fallen into sexual sin and speak as though their story has already ended.
We see someone worshiping through tears and assume their repentance is sincere, even though we cannot see the heart.
We see an impressive preacher and assume that public gifting guarantees private holiness.
Appearance can deceive in both directions.
The person who looks spiritually strong may be hiding serious sin.
The person who looks spiritually broken may be crying out to God with a humility we have forgotten.
This is why righteous judgment requires more than noticing behavior.
It requires truth, humility, fairness, discernment, and a refusal to pretend we possess God's complete knowledge.
Remember what God told Samuel when he was evaluating Jesse's sons:
“For man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.” — 1 Samuel 16:7 (KJV)
That does not mean outward actions are irrelevant.
Scripture repeatedly teaches that conduct matters.
It means we must never confuse our limited perspective with God's perfect knowledge.
We can evaluate words, actions, and teachings according to Scripture.
We cannot infallibly pronounce the final condition of another person's soul.
There is a difference.
And that difference matters eternally.
But now we must confront the other side of this conversation.
Because Matthew 7:1 is one of the most frequently quoted verses whenever someone feels confronted.
“Judge not, that ye be not judged.”
Those are the words of Jesus.
They deserve our full obedience.
But what did Jesus mean?
Continue reading.
“And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?” — Matthew 7:3 (KJV)
Jesus describes a person so concerned about a small obstruction in someone else's eye that he ignores a massive beam in his own.
It is almost absurd.
A man walking around with a wooden beam protruding from his face, volunteering to perform delicate eye surgery on someone else.
That is how ridiculous hypocrisy looks before God.
But Jesus does not finish by saying that the brother's problem must never be addressed.
He says:
“Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye.” — Matthew 7:5 (KJV)
Did you catch that?
First remove the beam. Then you will see clearly to help your brother.
Jesus condemns hypocritical judgment, not every form of moral discernment.
The goal is not to leave the other person wounded.
The goal is to become humble and clear-sighted enough to help.
That changes everything.
Because the purpose of biblical correction is not humiliation.
It is restoration.
It is not to prove that we are superior.
It is to help someone return to the One who can save.
And if your correction leaves you feeling proud of yourself and disgusted with the person you confronted, you need to examine whether your heart reflects the character of Christ.
Galatians 6:1 says:
“Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.”
Restore.
Not destroy.
In the original Greek, the verb translated “restore” is καταρτίζετε (katartizete), from katartizō, a word used for putting something into proper condition, repairing, or restoring.
The picture is not of a Christian standing over a fallen believer celebrating their failure.
It is of someone approaching carefully, humbly, and lovingly because a human soul matters.
A person is not a trophy for your theological argument.
A wounded believer is not content for your religious superiority.
A struggling sinner is not someone you get to publicly humiliate to prove that you are bold.
Truth without love can become cruelty.
And love without truth can become permission to remain in destruction.
Biblical love refuses both.
That is why Ephesians 4:15 speaks of “speaking the truth in love.”
Not truth instead of love.
Not love instead of truth.
Truth in love.
But there is a question many of us would rather avoid.
What happens when someone genuinely loves us enough to confront something we do not want to surrender?
What happens when the warning is biblical, the spirit is gentle, the concern is sincere, and we still respond with anger?
Sometimes we say “Don't judge me” because someone is being cruel.
And sometimes we say it because someone has touched an idol we desperately want to keep.
An unhealthy relationship.
A hidden habit.
Dishonesty we have renamed survival.
Bitterness we have renamed boundaries.
Pride we have renamed confidence.
Gossip we have renamed concern.
A refusal to forgive that we have renamed self-protection.
Not every difficult emotion is sin. Not every boundary is bitterness. Not every wounded person is rebellious.
But sometimes we know exactly what the Holy Spirit has been confronting, and we keep looking for someone who will tell us that obedience is unnecessary.
We do not want discernment.
We want agreement.
We do not want repentance.
We want relief from conviction.
We want Jesus to comfort us without challenging what is destroying us.
But the Savior who receives sinners also calls sinners to turn from sin.
Mark 1:15 records His proclamation:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
The Greek word translated “repent,” μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite), calls for repentance—a changed mind and orientation expressed in turning toward God.
Repentance is not simply feeling terrible about yourself.
It is not trying to earn forgiveness by becoming miserable enough.
It is responding to God's truth by turning from sin toward Him.
And the gospel is not that you can save yourself by making enough changes.
The gospel is that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, as proclaimed in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
Grace is not the reward for people who successfully repair themselves.
Grace is God's undeserved favor to people who need a Savior.
Yet that grace does not leave us unchanged.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains believers to deny ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace forgives.
Grace teaches.
Grace transforms.
And sometimes grace arrives through a conversation we initially resent.
Think about Nathan standing before King David.
David had committed adultery with Bathsheba and arranged circumstances that led to Uriah's death.
The king had power.
He had authority.
He could silence people.
But he could not silence God.
In 2 Samuel 12, Nathan confronted David through a story about a rich man who took a poor man's beloved lamb.
David became furious at the injustice.
He could clearly recognize evil when it belonged to someone else.
Then Nathan delivered the words that shattered his illusion.
“Thou art the man.” — 2 Samuel 12:7 (KJV)
Imagine the silence.
The king who could condemn another man's injustice was suddenly confronted with his own.
What would have happened if David had answered:
“Don't judge me, Nathan. Only God can judge me”?
But David did not ultimately defend his sin that way.
He confessed:
“I have sinned against the LORD.” — 2 Samuel 12:13 (KJV)
His repentance did not erase every earthly consequence of what he had done.
And his confession did not make his actions less grievous.
But David stopped pretending.
He acknowledged the truth.
That is where restoration begins.
Not when we become skilled at explaining why our sin is understandable.
Not when we find enough people to validate our choices.
But when we stop arguing with God.
Somebody reading this has spent months defending something God has been asking them to surrender.
You have explanations.
You have reasons.
Some of those reasons involve real suffering.
But deep down, beneath the explanations, you know there is a difference between asking God to heal your wounds and asking Him to approve the choices you are making because of them.
And perhaps the hardest prayer you can pray tonight is not “Lord, change everyone who has hurt me.”
Perhaps it is:
“Lord, show me what I have refused to see in myself.”
That prayer takes courage.
Because the truth can expose us before it comforts us.
But the God who exposes sin is also the God who offers mercy to repentant sinners.
Now consider another scene.
A woman stands before Jesus.
Religious accusers surround her.
She has been caught in adultery.
Her shame is public.
Her accusers are ready to use the law against her.
And Jesus is being tested.
John 8:1–11 records the encounter.

There is an important textual detail worth acknowledging: the account of the woman caught in adultery is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John and appears in different locations in parts of the manuscript tradition. Christians differ in how they assess its textual status. It should therefore be handled with that awareness rather than treated as an uncontested passage.
Still, the account presents a striking picture consistent with truths clearly taught elsewhere in Scripture.
Jesus says:
“He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.” — John 8:7 (KJV)
One by one, her accusers leave.
Then Jesus speaks to the woman.
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11 (KJV)
Do not miss the two truths held together in that sentence.
“Neither do I condemn thee.”
Mercy.
“Go, and sin no more.”
A call to leave sin.
Jesus did not treat her as disposable.
And He did not present adultery as harmless.
He refused to participate in the trap of her accusers, while the account also portrays Him calling her away from sin.
This is the balance we keep losing.
Some churches have become so afraid of appearing judgmental that they struggle to speak clearly about repentance.
Other churches have become so comfortable condemning sin that struggling people are afraid to confess what they are facing.
Neither reflects the fullness of biblical discipleship.
A faithful church should be a place where sin is taken seriously and repentant sinners are not treated as hopeless.
Where victims are protected, abuse is not concealed, and accountability is not confused with cruelty.
Where confession is met with truth, compassion, and appropriate responsibility.
Where leaders are not exempt from correction.
Where holiness is pursued without pretending that any Christian has reached sinless perfection.
Where the cross of Jesus Christ remains greater than our desire to look respectable.
Because the church is not a gathering of people who never needed mercy.
It is a gathering of people whose only hope is mercy through Christ.
And this is where another passage becomes essential.
In 1 Corinthians 5, the apostle Paul addresses serious, openly tolerated sexual immorality within the Corinthian church.
He does not instruct the believers to ignore the situation.
He calls them to exercise appropriate accountability within the believing community.
In verse 12, Paul asks:
“Do not ye judge them that are within?” — 1 Corinthians 5:12 (KJV)
The surrounding passage distinguishes accountability within the church from God's judgment of those outside it.
This is not permission for Christians to harass unbelievers or to become obsessed with policing the world.
Nor is it a license for abusive church discipline.
It establishes that the Christian community has a responsibility to take its own holiness seriously.
And even church discipline must be understood alongside the wider biblical commands concerning humility, fairness, repentance, forgiveness, and restoration.

In 2 Corinthians 2:6–8, Paul urges forgiveness, comfort, and reaffirmed love toward a disciplined person, lest excessive sorrow overwhelm him. The precise relationship of that individual to the situation in 1 Corinthians 5 is debated, but the restorative concern is unmistakable.
God's people must never confuse accountability with vengeance.
The objective is not to crush someone beneath shame.
It is to honor Christ, protect the community, and seek repentance and restoration wherever possible.
And there is another warning we cannot afford to ignore.
Jesus said:
“Judge not, and ye shall not be judged: condemn not, and ye shall not be condemned: forgive, and ye shall be forgiven.” — Luke 6:37 (KJV)
Scripture also teaches that believers must exercise discernment.
These commands are not contradictory.
The Christian must reject hypocritical, merciless condemnation while practicing just, humble, biblically grounded discernment.
We must never pretend to know more than we do.
We must not spread unverified accusations.
We must not use Scripture as a disguise for resentment.
We must not confuse our preferences with God's commandments.
And we must not treat every disagreement as evidence of spiritual rebellion.
Sometimes the righteous thing is to speak.
Sometimes it is to listen.
Sometimes it is to ask another question before making an accusation.
Sometimes it is to confront.
Sometimes it is to confess.
And sometimes the holiest words we can say are:
“I was wrong. Please forgive me.”
There is a particular kind of spiritual maturity that develops when you stop needing to win every confrontation.
You become more concerned with whether Christ is honored than whether you are proven right.
You learn to speak without enjoying another person's embarrassment.
You learn to receive correction without automatically assuming that correction is hatred.
You learn that not everyone who disagrees with you is persecuting you.
And not everyone who quotes Scripture is applying it faithfully.
You begin testing everything, including your own motives, against the Word of God.
That is not weakness.
That is growth.
But perhaps you are reading this from a very different place.
Perhaps someone used the Bible to shame you.
Perhaps a Christian leader exposed your private struggle in a way that humiliated you.
Perhaps people who knew nothing about your circumstances confidently announced what God thought of you.
Perhaps you walked away from church because the people who spoke most loudly about holiness showed so little compassion.
If that happened, the cruelty was not made righteous merely because someone attached a Bible verse to it.
You do not have to call spiritual abuse godly correction.
You do not have to remain in an unsafe situation to prove that you are forgiving.
And you do not have to pretend that serious wrongdoing is harmless.
Biblical forgiveness does not automatically eliminate the need for boundaries, justice, accountability, or protection.
But please do not allow someone's misrepresentation of Jesus to become your final understanding of Jesus.
Look at Christ Himself.
Look at how He confronted religious hypocrisy.
Look at how He welcomed the repentant.
Look at how He defended truth without becoming a servant of human pride.
Look at the cross.
There, the seriousness of sin and the immeasurable love of God meet in a way no human argument could ever accomplish.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had mastered obedience.
Not after our reputations were repaired.
Not after we learned to speak fluent Christian language.
Christ died for sinners.
And Romans 8:1 announces:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
That promise belongs to those who are in Christ.
It is not a declaration that sin is unimportant.
It is the glorious announcement that those united to Jesus Christ are no longer under condemnation because of His saving work.
This is why the gospel is greater than both self-righteousness and self-justification.
The self-righteous person says, “I am better than those sinners.”
The self-justifying person says, “My sin does not need to be confronted.”
But the repentant believer says:
“I am a sinner who needs Jesus, and His grace is too precious for me to keep pretending.”
That is where freedom begins.
Not in proving that you have never been wrong.
Not in collecting enough religious accomplishments to impress God.
Not in pretending that every choice you make is holy.
But in coming honestly to Christ.
You may have been the person who judged others harshly.
You may have been the person who rejected every loving warning.
You may have been both.
Many of us have.
And the beautiful thing about the gospel is that Jesus is not limited to saving one kind of sinner.
He can humble the proud.
He can restore the fallen.
He can forgive the repentant hypocrite.
He can receive the ashamed.
He can transform the person who has spent years hiding behind excuses.
He can teach the wounded believer how to trust again.
And He can take a life marked by scandal and write a testimony of grace.
Not because the scandal was good.
Not because consequences no longer matter.
But because sin and shame do not have to have the final word over someone who turns to Christ.
From scandal to grace is not the story of a God who pretends nothing happened.
It is the story of a Savior who knows exactly what happened and is mighty to redeem.
That is the heart of Gospel Warrior.
We are not here to build an audience of people who feel superior to everyone else.
We are here to proclaim Jesus Christ, open the Scriptures, call people to repentance, strengthen weary believers, and remind the broken that the grace of God is real.
And if this article has confronted something in you, do not rush past that moment.
Perhaps you need to apologize to someone you judged unfairly.
Perhaps you need to reach out to a brother or sister who has been drifting from Christ, not with accusations, but with tears, patience, and biblical truth.
Perhaps you need to confess a sin you have defended for years.
Perhaps you need to stop letting another person's hypocrisy become your excuse for remaining distant from Jesus.
Whatever the case, do not turn conviction into another passing emotion.
Bring it to God.
Pray with honesty.

“Lord Jesus, forgive me for the times I have used Your Word to wound others. Forgive me for the times I have used Your grace as an excuse to resist Your truth. Remove pride from my heart. Give me discernment without arrogance, courage without cruelty, and compassion without compromise. Teach me to receive correction, to repent sincerely, and to restore others gently. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Let my life reflect the mercy and holiness of my Savior. Amen.”
And if that prayer expresses something your heart has been struggling to say, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.
You do not need to expose private details or confess sensitive matters publicly. God hears the prayers you cannot explain in a comment section.
Your words may also remind another struggling believer that they are not alone.
And if this article brought someone to mind, consider sharing it directly with them—not as a weapon or a public accusation, but as an invitation to examine Scripture together.
Someone may be resisting a loving call to repentance.
Someone may be carrying shame they have never spoken about.
You cannot know every story behind the screen.
But you can help place a message about Jesus, truth, and grace within someone's reach.
Invite your family, your friends, the believer who has grown spiritually weary, and even the person who is still asking whether Christianity has anything meaningful to say about their life.
The truth of Scripture is worth studying carefully, not merely quoting when it supports what we already want to believe.
There is also a deeper way to stand alongside this ministry.
And certainly not because anyone must give money to prove that they love Jesus.
The gospel is not for sale, and your standing before God cannot be purchased.
But voluntary, generous support can be a meaningful act of Christian stewardship.

The apostle Paul taught that those who proclaim the gospel may receive material support for their ministry (1 Corinthians 9:14), while 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should be willing, not compelled.

It can function as a regular ministry offering in your personal giving plan, though it should not automatically be treated as equivalent to the biblical tithe, nor should it replace responsibilities to your local church, family, or those in need.
If you already give faithfully elsewhere, that is something to honor, not something we want you to neglect.
This is not merely about keeping a page active.
It is about sustaining the work behind the words.
The hours spent studying Scripture.
The care required to handle difficult passages responsibly.
The commitment to speak about repentance without abandoning grace.
The desire to reach the person who feels forgotten, the believer who is spiritually exhausted, and the seeker who has never clearly understood the gospel.
Those items are simply expressions of appreciation and practical resources. They are not spiritual rewards, and purchasing them is never a measure of someone's devotion to Christ.
Those free resources are part of the mission, too.
Because discipleship should never become something reserved only for people who can pay.
Keep reading.
Keep learning.
Keep sharing.
Keep growing in the Word.
Do it prayerfully, freely, and with a clear conscience before God.
It is how you will respond to Jesus Christ.
Because when the noise of social media fades, when the arguments end, when the comments stop arriving, and when nobody is watching what you do next, the question remains.
Are you willing to let the Word of God correct you?
Not just your enemies.
Not just the people you disagree with.
Not just the Christians whose failures disappoint you.
You.
Your assumptions.
Your motives.
Your secret compromises.
Your harshness.
Your excuses.
Your unwillingness to forgive.
Your fear of surrender.
Are you willing to stand before Scripture without demanding that it always agree with you?
And are you willing to let the same Savior who exposes your sin also lead you into the freedom of His grace?
One day, every human judgment will fade before the perfect judgment of God.

Jesus taught that the Father has entrusted judgment to the Son (John 5:22), and Acts 17:31 declares that God has appointed a day when He will judge the world in righteousness through the risen Christ.
That truth should make us humble.
It should make us serious about repentance.
It should make us careful with other people's souls.
And it should make the good news of Jesus Christ more precious than ever.
Because the final hope of the Christian is not that we judged everyone correctly.
It is not that we successfully defended ourselves against every accusation.
It is not that our religious reputation remained spotless.
Our hope is Jesus Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the dead.
The righteous Judge.
The merciful Savior.
The One before whom every excuse eventually fails, but in whom repentant sinners find forgiveness and life.
So the next time someone says, “Don't judge me,” remember that Jesus warned against hypocritical judgment.
And the next time someone uses that warning to silence every biblical correction, remember that Jesus also commanded righteous judgment.
Hold both truths.
Refuse hypocrisy.
Refuse compromise.
Speak truth with love.
Receive correction with humility.
Seek restoration instead of revenge.
And never forget that the cross stands as a reminder that sin is far too serious to excuse and God's grace is far too glorious to hide.
The most frightening blindness is not failing to see another person's sin—it is seeing everyone else's so clearly that you never notice how desperately you still need Jesus.
